recentItems.title: Al menos 47 muertos y más de 50 secuestrados en un ataque de bandas cerca de la capital de Haití
recentItems.description:
(26 Aug 2026) 
SOURCE - RESTRICTIONS

SLUG: Haiti Violencia SP 
Source: ASSOCIATED PRESS
No additional restrictions beyond those terms outlined in your license agreement.
 
Video de AP grabado por Pierre Luxama.
 
Al menos 47 muertos y más de 50 secuestrados en un ataque de bandas cerca de la capital de Haití 
 
——————————————————————————————————————————-
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Kenskoff, Haití - 25 de agosto de 2026
 
Al menos 47 personas murieron, entre ella s unos cinco niños, y más de 50 fueron secuestradas después de que hombres armados atacaran una comunidad que antes era pacífica, cerca de la capital de Haití, a principios de esta semana, según informaron el martes las Naciones Unidas. 
 
Se cree que el ataque del domingo en Kenscoff es uno de los mayores secuestros masivos en Haití en años recientes.
 
SOUNDBITE (Criollo haitiano) Jean Massillon, alcalde de Kenskoff: 
“Las bandas han matado a muchas personas en sus hogares”, dijo el alcalde de Kenscoff. “En un caso, miembros de bandas encerraron a personas dentro de una casa y le prendieron fuego con ellas adentro”.
 
En un video publicado en redes sociales, el líder de la pandilla lanzó una amenaza dirigida a Vladimir Paraison, director de la Policía Nacional: “si alguno de nuestros soldados resulta herido, los mataré a todos”, dijo en referencia a los rehenes.
 
Kenson Paul, un residente de Kenscoff de 17 años, relató que las bandas secuestraron a su padre, a su madre y a otros seis familiares. Su hermana, de 16 años, fue secuestrada y violada, pero logró escapar. El joven, estudiante de secundaria y agricultor, huyó a través de una ventana trasera. 
 
SOUNDBITE (Criollo haitiano) Kenson Paul, residente de Kenskoff: 
"Espero que el Estado pueda ayudar a que todos regresen a casa”, dijo el joven. “Somos simples agricultores. No estamos involucrados en nada". 
 
Hombres armados controlan cerca del 70% de Puerto Príncipe, extensas zonas del centro  de Haití y otras áreas.
 
Según estadísticas de la ONU publicadas el martes, entre enero y junio se reportaron  3.050 fallecidos y 1.400 heridos.
 
El ataque también podría ser una demostración de fuerza y un mensaje dirigido al gobierno y a la policía de Haití, justo cuando el país se prepara para celebrar elecciones generales el 13 de diciembre, las primeras en más de una década. 
 
ANNE MARIE GARCIA, ASSOCIATED PRESS

recentItems.title: Thousands of people celebrate Spain's tomato-throwing festival La Tomatina
recentItems.description:
(26 Aug 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY: 

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Bunol - 26 August 2026
1. Various of people participating in La Tomatina festival
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Mazhar Khan  (left) and Sanya Khan, 40-year-old couple from India:
“It was fantastic, absolutely well managed, we are from India, this is our first time being in La Tomatina. It has been a dream from over a decade, we have an Indian movie -  “Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara” (“You Only Live Once”) I saw it there and ever since then we wanted to come. “
Sanya Khan : "Bye"
3. Couple leaving
4. Group of friends at the festival covered in red pulp and tomato juice
5. SOUNDBITE (English) Gurpreet Singh, 31-year-old office worker, visitor from India:
“It was amazing, it was amazing, it was a lot of tomatoes, and we were planning for four years and we finally made it this year, It was really an amazing experience.”
6. Water splashed on participants from balconies 
7. SOUNDBITE (English) Luke Williams, 33-year-old programmer, visitor from UK:
“I’m from the UK, it was absolute chaos, I need glasses so I couldn't even see what was going on, I was just seeing red tomatoes everywhere.”
8. Couple covered in red pulp and tomato juice 
9. SOUNDBITE (English) Joanna Wytrzyszczewska, 32-year-old visitor from Poland:
“Way more crazy than we expected, we came because we were inspired by a movie, it was better than the movie.”
10. Mid of people on the ground 
11. Residents throwing water from balconies
12. Various of people at La Tomatina festival
STORYLINE:
Thousands of revelers descended on Buñol on Wednesday for the annual La Tomatina food fight, where they painted the small Spanish town red with up to 165 tons of overripe tomatoes.

Loaded trucks plodded through the crowd with people in their cargo beds throwing tomatoes at the revelers — who, in turn, hurled them at one another. 

Their white shirts soon turned pink and red while pop songs blasted from speakers. 

At one point, police appeared to use pepper spray to disperse an area of the crowd, but a festive vibe quickly resumed.

The messy melee takes place for over an hour in the town, where buildings are covered with tarps ahead of the festivities. 

Held on the last Wednesday of August, the festival traces its origins to a food fight in 1945.

La Tomatina became an annual tradition before Spanish dictator Gen. Francisco Franco banned it in the 1950s. 

Televised media attention in the 1980s helped turn the festival into a national event, and eventually, an international attraction.

More than 20,000 people had been expected to take part this year, with the Spanish news agency EFE reporting this week that roughly 40% of participants over the past three years have been tourists from outside Spain.

There has been a notable jump in visitors from India in recent years, following the 2011 Bollywood movie “Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara” (“You Only Live Once”), in which three friends take a road-trip through Spain during an extended bachelor party. 

The film recreated La Tomatina, introducing the festival to many Indians.

“It was amazing, it was amazing, it was a lot of tomatoes, and we were planning for four years and we finally made it this year, It was really an amazing experience," said Gurpreet Singh, a 31-year-old office worker, visiting from India. 

Similar tomato-flinging events have taken place in Florida, London, Amsterdam, the Colombian town of Sutamarchán and Hyderabad, India.

Non-local attendees pay 15 euros ($17.50) for a ticket. The first and only rule: Squash your tomatoes before hurling them to avoid injuries.

recentItems.title: Tributes left for Dolly Parton in Tennessee hometown of music and film icon
recentItems.description:
(26 Aug 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Sevierville, Tennessee - 26 August 2026
1. Wide of the flowers, bouquets and other tributes at Dolly Parton  statue's in Sevierville
2. Various of Dolly Parton statue paning down to plaque reading (English): Dolly, this statue of Dolly Parton was erected through the generosity of the people of Sevier County. Dedicated May 3, 1987."
3. Various of flower bouquets 
4. Wide of people standing near Dolly Parton statue 
5. Various of people paying tributes 
STORYLINE:
Fans across the country are mourning Dolly Parton, gathering at makeshift memorials and other places to celebrate the beloved singer, songwriter and philanthropist who died Tuesday in Nashville at 80.

The number of bouquets, drawings and other tributes are growing around the statue of the artist  on the front lawn of the county courthouse in her hometown of Sevierville, as a stream of fans visit the place to pay tribute to Parton. 

The country music icon whose soaring vibrato vocals, poignant songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, has died in Nashville. She was 80 years old.

“After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones,” her publicist, Marcel Pariseau, said in a statement Tuesday.

Known for her curvy physique, massive blond wigs and skin-tight outfits that served her self-deprecating wit, she was among the most beloved personalities in music and beyond — the rare celebrity whose appeal transcended generations, geography and politics.

She wrote hundreds of songs, including classics like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” that totaled more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams. Parton, who plucked bejeweled banjos, guitar and dulcimers with her long fingernails during performances, was a generous philanthropist and successful businesswoman whose projects included a theme park in the Smoky Mountain foothills near her birthplace.

Her career was forever influenced by her upbringing as one of 12 children born into what she called a “dirt poor” Tennessee family. She started her education nonprofit, Imagination Library, to send free books to children in Tennessee because her father, who quit school to work on the farm, struggled to learn to read. 

AP video shot by: Dylan Lovan

recentItems.description:
(26 Aug 2026)

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Buñol, Spain - 26 August 2026
1. Various of revelers throw tomatoes at each other
2. Various of festival staff inside big trucks throwing tomatoes to revellrs, through streets filled with red tomato juice and water 
3. Various of revelers soaked in red tomato juice, throwing tomatoes to each other
STORYLINE:
Thousands of revelers descended on Buñol on Wednesday for the annual La Tomatina food fight, where they painted the small Spanish town red with up to 165 tons of overripe tomatoes.

Loaded trucks plodded through the crowd with people in their cargo beds throwing tomatoes at the revelers — who, in turn, hurled them at one another. Their white shirts soon turned pink and red while pop songs blasted from speakers. At one point, police appeared to use pepper spray to disperse an area of the crowd, but a festive vibe quickly resumed.

The messy melee takes place for over an hour in the town, where buildings are covered with tarps ahead of the festivities. Held on the last Wednesday of August, the festival traces its origins to a food fight in 1945.

La Tomatina became an annual tradition before Spanish dictator Gen. Francisco Franco banned it in the 1950s. Televised media attention in the 1980s helped turn the festival into a national event, and eventually, an international attraction.

More than 20,000 people had been expected to take part this year, with the Spanish news agency EFE reporting this week that roughly 40% of participants over the past three years have been tourists from outside Spain.

There has been a notable jump in visitors from India in recent years, following the 2011 Bollywood movie “Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara” (“You Only Live Once”), in which three friends take a road-trip through Spain during an extended bachelor party. The film recreated La Tomatina, introducing the festival to many Indians.

The movie is what first drew Romail Khokhar, a 27-year-old from Mumbai, to Buñol. He was there on Wednesday morning, eager to participate in the food fight for his third time.

“I feel really great, actually. It's the best festival that I ever had, and I enjoy a lot here,” said Khokhar, who owns a clothing business.

Similar tomato-flinging events have taken place in Florida, London, Amsterdam, the Colombian town of Sutamarchán and Hyderabad, India.

Non-local attendees pay 15 euros ($17.50) for a ticket. The first and only rule: squash your tomatoes before hurling them to avoid injuries. Still, many participants don swimming goggles and earplugs for protection.

Once the hour is up, the sound of a cannon blast marks the end of festivities and crowds wash off at communal showers nearby. The town's streets are later hosed down.

Though stains on clothes can be permanent, the tomatoes' citric acid acts as a cleaning agent, often leaving Buñol's streets cleaner than before.

recentItems.title: US seeks to tap human appetite for seafood to fight growing numbers of invasive European green crabs
recentItems.description:
(26 Aug 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
York, Maine – 11 June 2026
1. Michael Masi, founder of a startup called Shell+Claw that studies and commercially harvests the invasive European green crabs, pilots his boat through steam York River as steam fog lifts around his vessel to check out his traps for the crustacean
2. SOUNDBITE (English) Michael Masi, European Green Crab Harvester: 
++PARTIALLY COVERED++
"Green crabs are a horribly invasive species that have been here for 200 years now. They eat up all the commercially valuable shellfish like oysters, clams, and mussels. They erode eelgrass beds and marsh bankings. And just about everyone hates them and we're trying to turn them into a... a premium seafood product.”
3. Masi empties a trap with the green crabs into a crate
4. Masi picks up a couple of green crabs from a crate
5. Close up of green crabs in a crate

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Portsmouth, New Hampshire – 26 May 2026
6. Volunteers are briefed before conducting a green crab survey along New Hampshire’s shores and salt marshes during an event known as the Great Green Crab Hunt, a periodic gathering conducted by University of New Hampshire Extension and New Hampshire Sea Grant
7. SOUNDBITE (English) Gabriela Bradt, University of New Hampshire: 
++PARTIALLY COVERED++
"They came over to the United States in the early 1800s in ballast water over from Europe... And even though they've been here for over 200 years, they aren't supposed to be here. So, they outcompete all of the native species such as lobsters, Jonah crabs, rock crabs, etc.”
8. Bradt recovers a green crab hidden underneath a rock and seaweed in the rocky intertidal zone during the survey
9. Bradt measures a green crab during the survey

ASSOCIATED PRESS
York, Maine – 11 June 2026
10. Close up of a green crab harvested by Masi
11. Aerial tracking shot of Masi’s boat harvesting green crabs
12. SOUNDBITE (English) Michael Masi, European Green Crab Harvester: 
++COVERED++
"One thing that has surprised me in being in this industry for the past five years is ... is just how much we can influence the ecological communities in the areas that we're fishing. We fished them (European green crabs) pretty hard in the York River, in Brave Boat Harbor, in Spruce Creek a little bit, and we do see that the ... the composition of the population changes. The crabs are a lot smaller now than they were when we started. Places where we never saw a lobster or a native rock crab ... our traps are coming up loaded with lobsters and rock crab."

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Cambridge, Massachusetts – 2 July 2026
13. A chef prepares soft-shell green crabs for cooking at Pagu, a restaurant that blends Japanese, Spanish and Taiwan influences

ASSOCIATED PRESS

recentItems.title: Traffic at Dubai’s airport dropped sharply during Iran war
recentItems.description:
(26 Aug 2026) 
RESTRICTION SUMMARY:

ASSOCIATED PRESS
Dubai, United Arab Emirates- 26 August 2026
1. Exterior of Terminal 3 at Dubai Airport
2. Passengers arriving to departure terminal
3. UAE flag
4. Passengers at the Departure terminal
5. SOUNDBITE (English), Paul Griffiths, CEO of Dubai Airports: 
“The events of the disruption, which lasted two months, that had an impact on traffic. However, the trajectory now is universally positive. If you look at our two home-based carriers, Emirates and Fly Dubai, their recovery in terms of capacity is in the 90s and percentile terms, and customers are not far behind that. So, that witnessing growth which suggests they'll be back to normal very, very shortly. We're just waiting for the overseas airlines, particularly from Europe, to restart operations and I'm very confident we'll be back to full operation in a very short space of time. Q3 and Q4 will be very strong for us and we're recovering growth incredibly quickly.”
6. Passengers heading to the smart gates
7. Close of Sign reading in Arabic and English “Departure gates, Smart Gates”
8. SOUNDBITE (English), Paul Griffiths, CEO of Dubai Airports: 
“The network that we operate here in the Gulf is incredibly resilient and is a significant volume. Close to 100 million people transit through Gulf airports and we have 45% of that market. And that hasn't actually changed. The split between people visiting or living in Dubai or transiting through the airport is roughly 50-50, which shows huge confidence in the ongoing operations that we serve here. So, as a force for global aviation, we are completely undeterred.”
9. Passengers passing near Departure screens
10. Close of screens
11. SOUNDBITE (English), Paul Griffiths, CEO of Dubai Airports: 
“The investment in the future continues. Already 10 million work hours in the last 15 months have been invested in our new airport, DWC, Al Maktoum International. 17,000 piles have been put into the ground, and we've got 45 million cubic meters of earth have already been moved, so. You don't need to look much further than that to know that we're absolutely committed to be a force for international aviation for a long time in the future.”
12. Various of passengers arriving
13. Top shot of arriving terminal
STORYLINE:
The CEO of Dubai Airports, one of the world’s busiest hubs, said Wednesday there was a sharp drop in passengers during the second quarter as the war with Iran disrupted air travel and prompted many travellers to choose routes that avoided the Middle East. 

The airport recorded 13 million passengers during the second quarter, for a 31.3% drop in first-half traffic over the same period last year with 31.5 million passengers overall. 

“The events of the disruption, which lasted two months, that had an impact on traffic. However, the trajectory now is universally positive. If you look at our two home-based carriers, Emirates and Fly Dubai, their recovery in terms of capacity is in the 90s and percentile terms, and customers are not far behind that. So, that witnessing growth which suggests they'll be back to normal very, very shortly, " said Paul Griffiths, the CEO of the two commercial airports in Dubai. 

Air traffic in the United Arab Emirates and elsewhere in the Gulf region was disrupted by shutdowns and restrictions after the United States and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28 to start the ongoing war. The airport itself suffered minor damage in attacks from Iran. 

Aircraft movements totalled 150,600 in the first half, down 32.1% year on year, with only 62,500 in the second quarter.



AP Video shot by: Bassam Hatoum

At one point, police appeared to use pepper spray to disperse an area of the crowd, but a festive vibe quickly resumed.

The messy melee takes place for over an hour in the town, where buildings are covered with tarps ahead of the festivities. Held on the last Wednesday of August, the festival traces its origins to a food fight in 1945.

La Tomatina became an annual tradition before Spanish dictator Gen. Francisco Franco banned it in the 1950s. Televised media attention in the 1980s helped turn the festival into a national event, and eventually, an international attraction.

More than 20,000 people had been expected to take part this year, with the Spanish news agency EFE reporting this week that roughly 40% of participants over the past three years have been tourists from outside Spain.

There has been a notable jump in visitors from India in recent years, following the 2011 Bollywood movie “Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara” (“You Only Live Once”), in which three friends take a road-trip through Spain during an extended bachelor party. The film recreated La Tomatina, introducing the festival to many Indians.

The movie is what first drew Romail Khokhar, a 27-year-old from Mumbai, to Buñol. He was there on Wednesday morning, eager to participate in the food fight for his third time.

“I feel really great, actually. It's the best festival that I ever had, and I enjoy a lot here,” said Khokhar, who owns a clothing business.

Similar tomato-flinging events have taken place in Florida, London, Amsterdam, the Colombian town of Sutamarchán and Hyderabad, India.

Non-local attendees pay 15 euros ($17.50) for a ticket. The first and only rule: squash your tomatoes before hurling them to avoid injuries. Still, many participants don swimming goggles and earplugs for protection.

Once the hour is up, the sound of a cannon blast marks the end of festivities and crowds wash off at communal showers nearby. The town's streets are later hosed down.

Though stains on clothes can be permanent, the tomatoes' citric acid acts as a cleaning agent, often leaving Buñol’s streets cleaner than before.

(26 Aug 2026)

SLUG: EE.UU. MEXICO SARGASSO SP 
Source: ASSOCIATED PRESS

Video de AP  realizado por Martín Silva Rey y producido por Fabiola Sánchez.
 
El impacto del sargazo: De refugio de vida marina a desafío costero 
____________________________________________
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Hollywood, Florida, EE.UU - 20 de agosto de 2026

A medida que el sargazo se acumula en las costas, cubre las aguas próximas a la orilla e impide que la luz solar llegue a las praderas de pastos marinos y a los arrecifes de coral. 
 
Los científicos estudian cómo cambia el ecosistema del sargazo al desplazarse desde el mar abierto hacia la costa.
 
Las algas en descomposición pueden reducir los niveles de oxígeno y liberar gases de olor desagradable, afectando la vida marina y ahuyentando a los turistas. 
 
Según los científicos, en julio se registraron unos 27 millones de toneladas métricas de sargazo en el Atlántico, el Caribe y el Golfo de México.

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Fort Pierce, Florida, EE.UU

SONIDO (inglés) Ellyn Willse, asistente de investigación de posgrado, Universidad Atlántica de Florida: 
“En 2025 se estimaron 38 millones de toneladas de sargazo”, dijo. “Este año, tuvimos ya unos 33 millones de toneladas, parece ser un problema creciente que seguiremos viendo”.
 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Tulum, México - 30 de julio de 2026
 
En las playas de Tulum, en la costa caribeña de México, el médico alemán Felix Strube junto a su hija, contempla los tramos de algas que cubren el agua.
 
SONIDO (Inglés) Felix Strube, turista alemán: 
“Fue un poco decepcionante”, dijo. “Se esperaban aguas turquesas”.
 
SONIDO (Español) Mercedes Hernández, turista de Ciudad de México: 
++Superpuesto con la imagen de la playa con sargazo++
"Es triste porque yo la conocí azul, azul, hermosa”.
 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Puerto Morelos, México - 31 de julio de 2026
 
En Puerto Morelos, la Marina de México ha desplegado cuadrillas de limpieza para retirar el sargazo antes de que llegue a las playas.
 
SONIDO (Español) Contralmirante Topiltzin Flores, responsable de la respuesta de la Marina mexicana ante el sargazo: 
++ superpuesto con la imagen de limpieza++
“El sargazo tenemos que aprender a vivir con el y ver la manera de sacarle un provecho, aprovechar la oportunidad que nos están dando de generar una economía circular.”
 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Puerto Morelos, México - 29 de julio de 2026
 
Una empresa mexicana está transformando el sargazo recolectado en productos como bioestimulantes agrícolas o ingredientes cosméticos. 
 
SOUNDBITE (Español) Rafael Carranza, jefe de operaciones y finanzas de Carbonwave: ++superpuesto en el video++
“El componente es sargazo, totalmente, un 99%”.
 
La proliferación de algas también afecta a personas cuyo sustento depende del mar.
 
ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Playa del Carmen, México - 29 de julio de 2026 
 
SOUNDBITE (Español) Roberto Verduzco, pescador: ++superpuesto con tomas de pescador recolectando peces ++
“Ahorita es una suerte que haya encontrado pescados, pero días atrás que han pasado no se podía absolutamente ni pescar”.

ASSOCIATED PRESS 
Loíza, Puerto Rico - 4 de agosto de 2025
 
Los científicos advierten que el sargazo proporciona un hábitat importante en alta mar, pero en la costa daña los ecosistemas marinos y amenaza el turismo, es un desafío  ambiental y económico para toda la región.
 
ANNE MARIE GARCIA, ASSOCIATED PRESS
